The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1–5] ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten stalks.﴾

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ That is, those who came from Yemen intending to destroy the Ka'bah, from Abyssinia (al-Habasha), and their leader was Abraha al-Habashi al-Ashram, as will be explained.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the hamza (interrogative particle) is to affirm his (ﷺ) seeing by denying its absence. The seeing is cognitive, meaning: Do you not know with a firm knowledge that approaches direct witnessing, through hearing widely transmitted reports and observing the manifest traces? The linking of the seeing to the manner of the act of Him, mighty and majestic, rather than to the act itself, by saying "Have you not seen what your Lord did…", is to magnify the event and to announce that it occurred in a dreadful manner and an amazing form, indicating the greatness of God's power, the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom, the might of His House, and the nobility of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

This is among the preparatory signs (irhasat, signs preceding prophethood), because it is related that the event took place in the year in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, as we will narrate.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ is a general explanation of what was done to them. That is: Did He not make their deceit and their effort to destroy the Ka'bah end in ruin and nullification of what they attempted, and destroy them with the utmost destruction?

Al-Razi said: Know that kayd (plot, scheming) is intending harm to another secretly. If it is said: Why did He call it (p-6260) a plot, when its matter was evident, for he openly declared that he would demolish the House? We say: Yes, but what was in his heart was worse than what he displayed, for he harbored envy toward the Arabs, and he wished to transfer the honor the Arabs had obtained through the Ka'bah, from them and their land, to himself and his own city.

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ that is, groups scattered, one following another from various directions. Ababil (flocks) is a plural with no singular, according to what Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' reported. Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy, claimed that he heard its singular as ibbalah, with a kasrah on the hamza and a shaddah on the letter ba', which is a bundle of firewood, used metaphorically for a flock of birds. Al-Kisa'i related from some grammarians that its singular is abul, and from others abil, by hearing, as Ibn Jarir transmitted.

The indefiniteness in "tayran" (birds) is either for belittlement, for however small it is, God's making is more wondrous and greater; or for magnification, as if He were saying: What birds are these that strike with small stones and never miss the target. This was noted by al-Razi.

﴿Striking them with stones of hard clay﴾ that is, of hardened clay. Ibn Wahb related from Ibn Zayd that what is meant by sijjil is the lowest heaven, because its name is Sijjil.

Ibn Jarir said: This saying of Ibn Zayd, we do not know of any validity for it, either in a report, in reason, or in language. The names of things are only known from a widespread language or from a report from God, may His remembrance be exalted.

﴿And He made them like eaten stalks﴾ Ibn Jarir said: like a crop that animals have eaten and then excreted, so it dried and its parts scattered; He likened the cutting apart of their joints and the dispersal of their limbs by the punishment that came upon them, to the scattering of the parts of dung that results from eating the crop.

Al-Shihab said: He did not mention the dung because of its vileness, so it came in accordance with the Qur'anic etiquette (adab). In it is a display of the disfigurement of their state.

(p-6261) Abu Muslim said: "al-'asf" (stalks) is the chaff, due to His saying: ﴿The possessor of the stalk and the basil﴾ [al-Rahman: 12], because the wind blows it away at threshing, separating it from the grain, and when it is eaten, it is destroyed and there is no return nor any protection in it. End of quote.

Among the possible readings of the verse is that the meaning is: like a crop whose grain has been eaten and only its straw remains, and the implied sense is "like a stalk whose grain has been eaten," just as one says "so-and-so is beautiful of face," so "eaten" is applied to "stalk" because its grain was eaten, since this meaning is known. Also among them is that the meaning of "eaten" is what is eaten, i.e., eaten by animals; it is said of anything fit for eating that it is "eaten." The meaning is: He made them like straw eaten by animals, in scattering, crumbling, and perishing. This was noted by al-Razi.

Notes:

The first: The cause for which God's punishment befell the companions of the elephant was the march of Abraha al-Habashi with his army and the elephant against the Sacred House of God, to destroy it. The event of the elephant is itself well known and widely transmitted, to the extent that they made it a starting point of dating by which they determined the times of events; they say: So-and-so was born in the Year of the Elephant, and such-and-such happened two years after the Year of the Elephant, and the like. The detailed account of its story is what Ibn Hisham transmitted: that Abraha al-Habashi was the governor of San'a for the Negus (al-Najashi), and he held the Christian faith. He built in San'a a church the like of which had not been seen in its time, then he wrote to the Negus: "Indeed I have built for you, O King, a church the like of which has not been built for any king before you, and I will not stop until I divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it." When the Arabs spoke of Abraha's letter to the Negus, a man from Kinanah became angry, so he went and came to the church and sat in it (i.e., he defiled it), then left and returned to his land. Abraha was informed of this and said: "Who did this?" It was said: "A man of the Arabs, from the people of this House to which the Arabs make pilgrimage in Mecca, heard your saying: 'I will divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it,' so he became angry, came and sat in it," meaning: it is not worthy of that. Abraha became furious at that and swore that he would march to the House until he demolished it. Then he ordered the Abyssinians, and they prepared and equipped themselves, then he set out and went with the elephant. (p-6262) The Arabs heard of that and considered it grave and dreadful, and they regarded fighting him as a duty upon them, when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'bah, the House of God, the Sacred. So a man came out to him who was one of the nobles and kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafar, and he called his people and those among the rest of the Arabs who responded to fight Abraha and to defend the House of God against what he intended of its demolition and destruction. Some responded to him. Then he confronted him, fought him, and Dhu Nafar and his companions were defeated, and he was brought as a captive. When he (Abraha) wanted to kill him, Dhu Nafar said: "O King! Do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than my death." So he spared him from killing and kept him bound in his custody—and Abraha was a clement man. Then Abraha proceeded on his course, seeking what he had set out for, until when he reached the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, and those who followed him from the tribes of the Arabs, and fought him. Abraha defeated him and Nufayl was taken as a captive, and he was brought. When he resolved to kill him, Nufayl said: "O King! Do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and these two hands of mine are yours over the tribe of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, by hearing and obedience." So he released him, and he went with him guiding him, until when he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib al-Thaqafi came out to him with the infantry of Thaqif, and they said to him: "O King! We are only your slaves, listening to you and obeying you; we have no opposition to you. This house of ours is not the House you seek"—they meant al-Lat—"you only seek the House that is in Mecca, and we will send with you someone who will guide you to it." So he let them be, (al-Lat was a house for them in al-Ta'if which they venerated, close to the veneration of the Ka'bah), and they sent with him Abu Righal to guide him on the way to Mecca. Abraha went out with Abu Righal until he halted him at al-Mughammas. When he halted him there, Abu Righal died there. The Arabs stoned his grave—it is the grave that people stone at al-Mughammas. When Abraha had alighted at al-Maghmas, he sent a man from the Abyssinians called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud with horses of his, until he reached Mecca, and he drove off to him the property of the people of Tihamah, from Quraysh and others, and he took two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who was then the greatest and chief of Quraysh. Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and whoever was in that sanctuary resolved to fight him, but then they realized that they had no power against him, so they abandoned that. Abraha sent Hinatah al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: "Ask about the chief of the people of this city and its noble, then say to him: The King says to you: I have not come to fight you; I have come only to demolish this House. If you do not stand against us in its defense with war, there is no need for me to shed your blood. And if he does not want to fight me, bring him to me." When Hinatah entered Mecca, he asked: "Who is the chief and noble of Quraysh?" It was said to him: "'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim." So he came to him and told him what Abraha had ordered him. 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "By God! We do not want to fight him, and we have no power for that. This is the Sacred House of God and the House of His Friend, peace be upon him"—(or as he said)—"if He defends it from him, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves between him and it, by God! We have no means of defending it."

(p-6263) Hinatah said to him: "Then come with me to him, for he has ordered me to bring you." So 'Abd al-Muttalib set out with him, and with him some of his sons, until he reached the encampment, and asked about Dhu Nafar, who was a friend of his, until he entered upon him in his prison. He said to him: "O Dhu Nafar! Do you have any help regarding what has befallen us?" Dhu Nafar said to him: "What help can a captive in the hands of a king expect, who waits to kill him morning and evening? I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that Unays, the elephant-keeper, is my friend. I will send to him and charge him concerning you, and I will magnify your right upon him, and ask him to seek permission for you from the King, so that he may speak to him as you wish and intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do that." He said: "That is enough for me." So Dhu Nafar sent to Unays and said to him: "'Abd al-Muttalib is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the spring of Mecca: he feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountaintops. The King has taken from him two hundred camels. So seek permission for him to enter upon him, and intercede for him with him as much as you can." He said: "I will do that." So Unays spoke to Abraha and said to him: "O King! This is the chief of Quraysh at your door seeking permission to see you, and he is the owner of the spring of Mecca; he feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountaintops. So permit him to enter upon you, that he may speak to you about his need." He said: So Abraha gave him permission. He said: 'Abd al-Muttalib was the most handsome, the most beautiful, and the greatest of people. When Abraha saw him, he esteemed him and honored him and was too generous to let him sit beneath him, and he disliked that the Abyssinians should see him seat him with himself on his royal throne. So Abraha descended from his throne and sat on his carpet, and seated him beside himself on it, then he said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" The interpreter said that to him. He said: "My need is that the King return to me the two hundred camels he took for me." When he said that, Abraha said to his interpreter: "Say to him: You had impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you since you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels I took from you, and leave a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish, and you do not speak to me about it?" 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the owner of the camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "And who would be able to prevent me?" He said: (p-6264) "You and that." It is said, according to what the scholars claim, that Ma'mar ibn Nafathah, chief of Bani Bakr, and Khuwaylid ibn Wathilah, chief of Hudhayl, had gone with 'Abd al-Muttalib to Abraha when he sent Hinatah; they offered Abraha a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused them. God knows best whether that was so or not.

Abraha returned to Abd al-Muttalib the camels that he had seized from him. When they had departed from him, Abd al-Muttalib went back to Quraysh, informed them of the news, and ordered them to leave Makkah and take refuge in the mountain peaks and the ravines, fearing for them the harm of the army. Then Abd al-Muttalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and a group of Quraysh stood with him, calling upon Allah and seeking His aid against Abraha and his army. Abd al-Muttalib, while holding the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, said:

؎O Allah, indeed the servant defends his property, so defend Your sanctuary.
؎Let not their cross and their stratagems prevail against Your stratagem, ever.
؎If You leave them and our qiblah, then it is a matter that is clear to You.

Then Abd al-Muttalib let go of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and he and those with him from Quraysh set off for the mountain peaks, where they took refuge, waiting to see what Abraha would do to Makkah when he entered it. When morning came, Abraha prepared to enter Makkah. He readied his elephant and arrayed his army, and Abraha was resolved to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they directed the elephant toward Makkah, Nufayl ibn Habib came and stood beside the elephant, took hold of its ear, and said to it: "Kneel down, or go back safely from where you came, for you are in the sacred land of Allah." Then he let go of its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl set off running until he climbed up the mountain.

They struck the elephant so that it would rise, and they struck its head so that it would rise, but it refused. They inserted their hooks into its sensitive parts and pierced it with them, that is, they drew blood, so that it would rise, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it rose and trotted. They turned it toward Syria, and it did the same. They turned it toward the east, and it did the same. They turned it toward Makkah, and it knelt down. Then Allah the Exalted sent birds from the sea, like the swallows and the bullfinches, each bird carrying three stones: a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. They did not strike anyone except that he perished, though not all of them were struck. They fled in flight, rushing along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl so that he might guide them to the road to Yemen. When Nufayl saw what Allah had sent down upon them of His vengeance, he said:

؎Where is the escape, when the Seeker is God, and the cut-nosed one is defeated, and not the victor?

Thus they fell scattered along every road and perished at every place of descent, at every watering place. Abraha himself was struck in his body, and they carried him with them while he fell apart one joint at a time. Whenever a joint fell from him, a discharge followed it, flowing with pus and blood, until they brought him to Sana'a, where he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.

Ibn Ishaq said: Ya'qub ibn Utbah narrated to me that he related that the first appearance of measles and smallpox in the land of the Arabs was in that year.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), among what Allah counted against Quraysh of His blessing and favour upon them was that He warded off from them the matter of the Abyssinians, so that their affair and their period might endure. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ to the end of the surah.

Then Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah turned back the Abyssinians from Makkah and struck them with the vengeance with which He struck them, the Arabs held Quraysh in great esteem and said: "They are the People of Allah; Allah fought on their behalf and spared them the burden of their enemy." They composed poems on this, mentioning in them what Allah had done to the Abyssinians and what He had averted from Quraysh of their plotting. Then he went on to set down the odes on this matter.

I have chosen to cite what Ibn Hisham narrated from Ibn Ishaq, because it is the best in its narration and the most eloquent in its composition, since it preserves the pure Arabic speech of the most distinguished of its poets. May Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him.

Second admonition: The account is attributed to the elephant and became famous through it, because they brought the elephant with them for the purpose of violence and destruction. For if their plot had succeeded for its two leaders, the elephant would have been their effective hand and their far-reaching arrow. This is because the tyrants of the lands in which the elephant is found take it as an instrument of violence and vengeance. When they are angry with an enemy, they seize him; or with a vizier, they bind him; or with a city, they besiege its fortress, and they send the elephant against the house of the one with whom they are angry, or against his fortress, and it strikes the edifice with its head and tusk and tears it down, and it demolishes the foundations of the building. It is more effective than mattocks and axes, and greater in terror and awe in souls. Sometimes they throw the one who has incurred their wrath before it, and it works its tusk upon him, wraps its trunk around him, and lifts him, and it mutilates him in a manner more violent and more exemplary. Some of the descendants of the kings of Afghanistan related to me some strange accounts of these Jahili atrocities when he stayed for a period in Syria.

Third: Al-Qashani said: The story of the companions of the elephant is well known, and its event is close to the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). It is one of the signs of Allah and a trace of His wrath against whoever dared to violate His sanctuary by desecrating its sacred things. The inspiration of birds and beasts is closer [to acceptance] than the inspiration of man, because their souls are simple. The effect of stones through a property that Allah the Exalted placed in them is not strange. Whoever has perceived the world of power, and the veil of wisdom has been uncovered for him, will recognise similar things.

He said: Something similar occurred in our time, in the rats' domination over the city of Abiward, the ruin of their crops, and their return into the desert to the bank of the Oxus, where each of them took a piece of wood from the thicket on the bank of its river, rode upon it, and crossed by it over the river.

Fourth: Imam al-Mawardi said in (A'lam al-Nubuwwah): The signs of kingship are dazzling, and the proofs of prophethood are overpowering. Their beginnings bear witness to their outcomes, so falsehood is not mixed with truth in them, nor is the pretender confused with the rightly guided. In accordance with their strength and their spread are their tidings and their warnings. When the birth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew near, the signs of his prophethood came in succession, and the signs of his blessing appeared. Among the greatest of them in importance, the clearest in proof, and the most widely known in witness and report was the companions of the elephant. The Negus sent them from the land of Abyssinia with the bulk of his army against Makkah, to kill its men, take captive its offspring, and demolish the Ka'bah. The sign of the Messenger in the story of the elephant was that he was in the womb of his mother in Makkah at that time, for he was born fifty days after the elephant. His sign in this was in two respects:

The first: If they had prevailed, they would have taken captives and enslaved, so Allah the Exalted destroyed them to protect His Messenger from being subjected to captivity, as a foetus and as an infant. The second: Quraysh did not possess such devotion to God that would merit their repelling the companions of the elephant from them, nor were they a people of scripture, for they were among worshippers of idols, adherents of paganism, proponents of heresy, or deniers of resurrection. Rather, it was because of what Allah the Exalted willed of the manifestation of Islam, as the foundation of prophethood and the exaltation of the Ka'bah, and that He should make it the qiblah for prayer and the place of rites for the Hajj.

If it is said: How was the Ka'bah prevented from being the qiblah and the place of rites before this, but al-Hajjaj was not prevented from demolishing it, even though it had already become the qiblah and the place of rites, until he burned it and set up the catapult against it?

It is said: The act of al-Hajjaj came after the religion had become firmly established, so it had no need of the signs of its foundation. The companions of the elephant came before the manifestation of prophethood, so the prevention from it became a sign for the foundation of prophethood and the coming of the message. Moreover, the Messenger had given warning of its demolition, so the demolition became a sign after the prevention had been a sign. Therefore its ruling differed in the two situations. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

When what Allah the Exalted had done to the army of the elephant spread among the Arabs, they came to revere the Sanctuary and hold it in great awe, and its sanctity increased in souls. They submitted to Quraysh in obedience and said: "They are the People of Allah; He fought on their behalf and spared them the plotting of their enemy." So they increased them in honour and exaltation, and they became leaders who were obeyed, and chiefs who were followed. The companions of the elephant became a proverb among those who remained behind. The matter of the elephant was a deterrent to every transgressor and a repellent to every tyrant. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived at the same time, in his prophetic period and after his migration, with a group who had witnessed the elephant and the flock of birds, among them Hakim ibn Hizam, Hatib ibn Abd al-Uzza, and Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah, because each of these lived one hundred and twenty years: sixty of them in the Jahiliyyah and sixty in Islam. End of quote.

Fifth: Reference to the story of the elephant occurs in many authentic hadiths. Al-Bukhari narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) came near on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, at the pass by which one descends upon Quraysh, his she-camel knelt down. They drove her on, but she insisted, so they said: "Al-Qaswa has stopped," that is, she became stubborn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-Qaswa has not stopped, nor is that her habit, but the one who holds back the elephant has held her back." Ibn al-Athir said in (al-Nihayah): It is the elephant of Abraha the Abyssinian, who came intending to destroy the Ka'bah, but Allah held back the elephant so that it did not enter the Sanctuary, and turned its head back from where it had come. He means that Allah held back the she-camel of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he reached al-Hudaybiyah, so it did not advance and did not enter the Sanctuary, because he intended to enter Makkah with the Muslims.

Also in the two Sahihs: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: 'Indeed Allah held back the elephant from Makkah and gave His Messenger and the believers power over it. Indeed its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday. Let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent.'"

The first: The cause for which God's punishment befell the companions of the elephant was the march of Abraha al-Habashi with his army and the elephant against the Sacred House of God, to destroy it. The event of the elephant is itself well known and widely transmitted, to the extent that they made it a starting point of dating by which they determined the times of events; they say: So-and-so was born in the Year of the Elephant, and such-and-such happened two years after the Year of the Elephant, and the like. The detailed account of its story is what Ibn Hisham transmitted: that Abraha al-Habashi was the governor of San'a for the Negus (al-Najashi), and he held the Christian faith. He built in San'a a church the like of which had not been seen in its time, then he wrote to the Negus: "Indeed I have built for you, O King, a church the like of which has not been built for any king before you, and I will not stop until I divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it." When the Arabs spoke of Abraha's letter to the Negus, a man from Kinanah became angry, so he went and came to the church and sat in it (i.e., he defiled it), then left and returned to his land. Abraha was informed of this and said: "Who did this?" It was said: "A man of the Arabs, from the people of this House to which the Arabs make pilgrimage in Mecca, heard your saying: 'I will divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs to it,' so he became angry, came and sat in it," meaning: it is not worthy of that. Abraha became furious at that and swore that he would march to the House until he demolished it. Then he ordered the Abyssinians, and they prepared and equipped themselves, then he set out and went with the elephant. (p-6262) The Arabs heard of that and considered it grave and dreadful, and they regarded fighting him as a duty upon them, when they heard that he intended to demolish the Ka'bah, the House of God, the Sacred. So a man came out to him who was one of the nobles and kings of Yemen, called Dhu Nafar, and he called his people and those among the rest of the Arabs who responded to fight Abraha and to defend the House of God against what he intended of its demolition and destruction. Some responded to him. Then he confronted him, fought him, and Dhu Nafar and his companions were defeated, and he was brought as a captive. When he (Abraha) wanted to kill him, Dhu Nafar said: "O King! Do not kill me, for perhaps my remaining with you will be better for you than my death." So he spared him from killing and kept him bound in his custody—and Abraha was a clement man. Then Abraha proceeded on his course, seeking what he had set out for, until when he reached the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, and those who followed him from the tribes of the Arabs, and fought him. Abraha defeated him and Nufayl was taken as a captive, and he was brought. When he resolved to kill him, Nufayl said: "O King! Do not kill me, for I am your guide in the land of the Arabs, and these two hands of mine are yours over the tribe of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahis, by hearing and obedience." So he released him, and he went with him guiding him, until when he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib al-Thaqafi came out to him with the infantry of Thaqif, and they said to him: "O King! We are only your slaves, listening to you and obeying you; we have no opposition to you. This house of ours is not the House you seek"—they meant al-Lat—"you only seek the House that is in Mecca, and we will send with you someone who will guide you to it." So he let them be, (al-Lat was a house for them in al-Ta'if which they venerated, close to the veneration of the Ka'bah), and they sent with him Abu Righal to guide him on the way to Mecca. Abraha went out with Abu Righal until he halted him at al-Mughammas. When he halted him there, Abu Righal died there. The Arabs stoned his grave—it is the grave that people stone at al-Mughammas. When Abraha had alighted at al-Maghmas, he sent a man from the Abyssinians called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud with horses of his, until he reached Mecca, and he drove off to him the property of the people of Tihamah, from Quraysh and others, and he took two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, who was then the greatest and chief of Quraysh. Quraysh, Kinanah, Hudhayl, and whoever was in that sanctuary resolved to fight him, but then they realized that they had no power against him, so they abandoned that. Abraha sent Hinatah al-Himyari to Mecca and said to him: "Ask about the chief of the people of this city and its noble, then say to him: The King says to you: I have not come to fight you; I have come only to demolish this House. If you do not stand against us in its defense with war, there is no need for me to shed your blood. And if he does not want to fight me, bring him to me." When Hinatah entered Mecca, he asked: "Who is the chief and noble of Quraysh?" It was said to him: "'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim." So he came to him and told him what Abraha had ordered him. 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "By God! We do not want to fight him, and we have no power for that. This is the Sacred House of God and the House of His Friend, peace be upon him"—(or as he said)—"if He defends it from him, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves between him and it, by God! We have no means of defending it."

(p-6263) Hinatah said to him: "Then come with me to him, for he has ordered me to bring you." So 'Abd al-Muttalib set out with him, and with him some of his sons, until he reached the encampment, and asked about Dhu Nafar, who was a friend of his, until he entered upon him in his prison. He said to him: "O Dhu Nafar! Do you have any help regarding what has befallen us?" Dhu Nafar said to him: "What help can a captive in the hands of a king expect, who waits to kill him morning and evening? I have no help in anything that has befallen you, except that Unays, the elephant-keeper, is my friend. I will send to him and charge him concerning you, and I will magnify your right upon him, and ask him to seek permission for you from the King, so that he may speak to him as you wish and intercede for you with him for good, if he is able to do that." He said: "That is enough for me." So Dhu Nafar sent to Unays and said to him: "'Abd al-Muttalib is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the spring of Mecca: he feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountaintops. The King has taken from him two hundred camels. So seek permission for him to enter upon him, and intercede for him with him as much as you can." He said: "I will do that." So Unays spoke to Abraha and said to him: "O King! This is the chief of Quraysh at your door seeking permission to see you, and he is the owner of the spring of Mecca; he feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountaintops. So permit him to enter upon you, that he may speak to you about his need." He said: So Abraha gave him permission. He said: 'Abd al-Muttalib was the most handsome, the most beautiful, and the greatest of people. When Abraha saw him, he esteemed him and honored him and was too generous to let him sit beneath him, and he disliked that the Abyssinians should see him seat him with himself on his royal throne. So Abraha descended from his throne and sat on his carpet, and seated him beside himself on it, then he said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" The interpreter said that to him. He said: "My need is that the King return to me the two hundred camels he took for me." When he said that, Abraha said to his interpreter: "Say to him: You had impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost interest in you since you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels I took from you, and leave a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, which I have come to demolish, and you do not speak to me about it?" 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the owner of the camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "And who would be able to prevent me?" He said: (p-6264) "You and that." It is said, according to what the scholars claim, that Ma'mar ibn Nafathah, chief of Bani Bakr, and Khuwaylid ibn Wathilah, chief of Hudhayl, had gone with 'Abd al-Muttalib to Abraha when he sent Hinatah; they offered Abraha a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused them. God knows best whether that was so or not.

Abraha returned to Abd al-Muttalib the camels that he had seized from him. When they had departed from him, Abd al-Muttalib went back to Quraysh, informed them of the news, and ordered them to leave Makkah and take refuge in the mountain peaks and the ravines, fearing for them the harm of the army. Then Abd al-Muttalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and a group of Quraysh stood with him, calling upon Allah and seeking His aid against Abraha and his army. Abd al-Muttalib, while holding the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, said:

؎O Allah, indeed the servant defends his property, so defend Your sanctuary.
؎Let not their cross and their stratagems prevail against Your stratagem, ever.
؎If You leave them and our qiblah, then it is a matter that is clear to You.

Then Abd al-Muttalib let go of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and he and those with him from Quraysh set off for the mountain peaks, where they took refuge, waiting to see what Abraha would do to Makkah when he entered it. When morning came, Abraha prepared to enter Makkah. He readied his elephant and arrayed his army, and Abraha was resolved to demolish the House and then return to Yemen. When they directed the elephant toward Makkah, Nufayl ibn Habib came and stood beside the elephant, took hold of its ear, and said to it: "Kneel down, or go back safely from where you came, for you are in the sacred land of Allah." Then he let go of its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl set off running until he climbed up the mountain.

They struck the elephant so that it would rise, and they struck its head so that it would rise, but it refused. They inserted their hooks into its sensitive parts and pierced it with them, that is, they drew blood, so that it would rise, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it rose and trotted. They turned it toward Syria, and it did the same. They turned it toward the east, and it did the same. They turned it toward Makkah, and it knelt down. Then Allah the Exalted sent birds from the sea, like the swallows and the bullfinches, each bird carrying three stones: a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. They did not strike anyone except that he perished, though not all of them were struck. They fled in flight, rushing along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl so that he might guide them to the road to Yemen. When Nufayl saw what Allah had sent down upon them of His vengeance, he said:

؎Where is the escape, when the Seeker is God, and the cut-nosed one is defeated, and not the victor?

Thus they fell scattered along every road and perished at every place of descent, at every watering place. Abraha himself was struck in his body, and they carried him with them while he fell apart one joint at a time. Whenever a joint fell from him, a discharge followed it, flowing with pus and blood, until they brought him to Sana'a, where he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.

Ibn Ishaq said: Ya'qub ibn Utbah narrated to me that he related that the first appearance of measles and smallpox in the land of the Arabs was in that year.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), among what Allah counted against Quraysh of His blessing and favour upon them was that He warded off from them the matter of the Abyssinians, so that their affair and their period might endure. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ to the end of the surah.

Then Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah turned back the Abyssinians from Makkah and struck them with the vengeance with which He struck them, the Arabs held Quraysh in great esteem and said: "They are the People of Allah; Allah fought on their behalf and spared them the burden of their enemy." They composed poems on this, mentioning in them what Allah had done to the Abyssinians and what He had averted from Quraysh of their plotting. Then he went on to set down the odes on this matter.

I have chosen to cite what Ibn Hisham narrated from Ibn Ishaq, because it is the best in its narration and the most eloquent in its composition, since it preserves the pure Arabic speech of the most distinguished of its poets. May Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him.

Second admonition: The account is attributed to the elephant and became famous through it, because they brought the elephant with them for the purpose of violence and destruction. For if their plot had succeeded for its two leaders, the elephant would have been their effective hand and their far-reaching arrow. This is because the tyrants of the lands in which the elephant is found take it as an instrument of violence and vengeance. When they are angry with an enemy, they seize him; or with a vizier, they bind him; or with a city, they besiege its fortress, and they send the elephant against the house of the one with whom they are angry, or against his fortress, and it strikes the edifice with its head and tusk and tears it down, and it demolishes the foundations of the building. It is more effective than mattocks and axes, and greater in terror and awe in souls. Sometimes they throw the one who has incurred their wrath before it, and it works its tusk upon him, wraps its trunk around him, and lifts him, and it mutilates him in a manner more violent and more exemplary. Some of the descendants of the kings of Afghanistan related to me some strange accounts of these Jahili atrocities when he stayed for a period in Syria.

Third: Al-Qashani said: The story of the companions of the elephant is well known, and its event is close to the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). It is one of the signs of Allah and a trace of His wrath against whoever dared to violate His sanctuary by desecrating its sacred things. The inspiration of birds and beasts is closer [to acceptance] than the inspiration of man, because their souls are simple. The effect of stones through a property that Allah the Exalted placed in them is not strange. Whoever has perceived the world of power, and the veil of wisdom has been uncovered for him, will recognise similar things.

He said: Something similar occurred in our time, in the rats' domination over the city of Abiward, the ruin of their crops, and their return into the desert to the bank of the Oxus, where each of them took a piece of wood from the thicket on the bank of its river, rode upon it, and crossed by it over the river.

Fourth: Imam al-Mawardi said in (A'lam al-Nubuwwah): The signs of kingship are dazzling, and the proofs of prophethood are overpowering. Their beginnings bear witness to their outcomes, so falsehood is not mixed with truth in them, nor is the pretender confused with the rightly guided. In accordance with their strength and their spread are their tidings and their warnings. When the birth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew near, the signs of his prophethood came in succession, and the signs of his blessing appeared. Among the greatest of them in importance, the clearest in proof, and the most widely known in witness and report was the companions of the elephant. The Negus sent them from the land of Abyssinia with the bulk of his army against Makkah, to kill its men, take captive its offspring, and demolish the Ka'bah. The sign of the Messenger in the story of the elephant was that he was in the womb of his mother in Makkah at that time, for he was born fifty days after the elephant. His sign in this was in two respects:

The first: If they had prevailed, they would have taken captives and enslaved, so Allah the Exalted destroyed them to protect His Messenger from being subjected to captivity, as a foetus and as an infant. The second: Quraysh did not possess such devotion to God that would merit their repelling the companions of the elephant from them, nor were they a people of scripture, for they were among worshippers of idols, adherents of paganism, proponents of heresy, or deniers of resurrection. Rather, it was because of what Allah the Exalted willed of the manifestation of Islam, as the foundation of prophethood and the exaltation of the Ka'bah, and that He should make it the qiblah for prayer and the place of rites for the Hajj.

If it is said: How was the Ka'bah prevented from being the qiblah and the place of rites before this, but al-Hajjaj was not prevented from demolishing it, even though it had already become the qiblah and the place of rites, until he burned it and set up the catapult against it?

It is said: The act of al-Hajjaj came after the religion had become firmly established, so it had no need of the signs of its foundation. The companions of the elephant came before the manifestation of prophethood, so the prevention from it became a sign for the foundation of prophethood and the coming of the message. Moreover, the Messenger had given warning of its demolition, so the demolition became a sign after the prevention had been a sign. Therefore its ruling differed in the two situations. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

When what Allah the Exalted had done to the army of the elephant spread among the Arabs, they came to revere the Sanctuary and hold it in great awe, and its sanctity increased in souls. They submitted to Quraysh in obedience and said: "They are the People of Allah; He fought on their behalf and spared them the plotting of their enemy." So they increased them in honour and exaltation, and they became leaders who were obeyed, and chiefs who were followed. The companions of the elephant became a proverb among those who remained behind. The matter of the elephant was a deterrent to every transgressor and a repellent to every tyrant. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived at the same time, in his prophetic period and after his migration, with a group who had witnessed the elephant and the flock of birds, among them Hakim ibn Hizam, Hatib ibn Abd al-Uzza, and Nawfal ibn Mu'awiyah, because each of these lived one hundred and twenty years: sixty of them in the Jahiliyyah and sixty in Islam. End of quote.

Fifth: Reference to the story of the elephant occurs in many authentic hadiths. Al-Bukhari narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) came near on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, at the pass by which one descends upon Quraysh, his she-camel knelt down. They drove her on, but she insisted, so they said: "Al-Qaswa has stopped," that is, she became stubborn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Al-Qaswa has not stopped, nor is that her habit, but the one who holds back the elephant has held her back." Ibn al-Athir said in (al-Nihayah): It is the elephant of Abraha the Abyssinian, who came intending to destroy the Ka'bah, but Allah held back the elephant so that it did not enter the Sanctuary, and turned its head back from where it had come. He means that Allah held back the she-camel of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he reached al-Hudaybiyah, so it did not advance and did not enter the Sanctuary, because he intended to enter Makkah with the Muslims.

Also in the two Sahihs: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: 'Indeed Allah held back the elephant from Makkah and gave His Messenger and the believers power over it. Indeed its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday. Let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent.'"

Surat al-Fil

Meccan, and its verses are five.

[p-6259] In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1–5] ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten stalks.﴾

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ That is, those who came from Yemen intending to destroy the Ka'bah, from Abyssinia (al-Habasha), and their leader was Abraha al-Habashi al-Ashram, as will be explained.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the hamza (interrogative particle) is to affirm his (ﷺ) seeing by denying its absence. The seeing is cognitive, meaning: Do you not know with a firm knowledge that approaches direct witnessing, through hearing widely transmitted reports and observing the manifest traces? The linking of the seeing to the manner of the act of Him, mighty and majestic, rather than to the act itself, by saying "Have you not seen what your Lord did…", is to magnify the event and to announce that it occurred in a dreadful manner and an amazing form, indicating the greatness of God's power, the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom, the might of His House, and the nobility of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

This is among the preparatory signs (irhasat, signs preceding prophethood), because it is related that the event took place in the year in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, as we will narrate.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ is a general explanation of what was done to them. That is: Did He not make their deceit and their effort to destroy the Ka'bah end in ruin and nullification of what they attempted, and destroy them with the utmost destruction?

Al-Razi said: Know that kayd (plot, scheming) is intending harm to another secretly. If it is said: Why did He call it (p-6260) a plot, when its matter was evident, for he openly declared that he would demolish the House? We say: Yes, but what was in his heart was worse than what he displayed, for he harbored envy toward the Arabs, and he wished to transfer the honor the Arabs had obtained through the Ka'bah, from them and their land, to himself and his own city.

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ that is, groups scattered, one following another from various directions. Ababil (flocks) is a plural with no singular, according to what Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' reported. Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy, claimed that he heard its singular as ibbalah, with a kasrah on the hamza and a shaddah on the letter ba', which is a bundle of firewood, used metaphorically for a flock of birds. Al-Kisa'i related from some grammarians that its singular is abul, and from others abil, by hearing, as Ibn Jarir transmitted.

The indefiniteness in "tayran" (birds) is either for belittlement, for however small it is, God's making is more wondrous and greater; or for magnification, as if He were saying: What birds are these that strike with small stones and never miss the target. This was noted by al-Razi.

﴿Striking them with stones of hard clay﴾ that is, of hardened clay. Ibn Wahb related from Ibn Zayd that what is meant by sijjil is the lowest heaven, because its name is Sijjil.

Ibn Jarir said: This saying of Ibn Zayd, we do not know of any validity for it, either in a report, in reason, or in language. The names of things are only known from a widespread language or from a report from God, may His remembrance be exalted.

﴿And He made them like eaten stalks﴾ Ibn Jarir said: like a crop that animals have eaten and then excreted, so it dried and its parts scattered; He likened the cutting apart of their joints and the dispersal of their limbs by the punishment that came upon them, to the scattering of the parts of dung that results from eating the crop.

Al-Shihab said: He did not mention the dung because of its vileness, so it came in accordance with the Qur'anic etiquette (adab). In it is a display of the disfigurement of their state.

(p-6261) Abu Muslim said: "al-'asf" (stalks) is the chaff, due to His saying: ﴿The possessor of the stalk and the basil﴾ [al-Rahman: 12], because the wind blows it away at threshing, separating it from the grain, and when it is eaten, it is destroyed and there is no return nor any protection in it. End of quote.

Among the possible readings of the verse is that the meaning is: like a crop whose grain has been eaten and only its straw remains, and the implied sense is "like a stalk whose grain has been eaten," just as one says "so-and-so is beautiful of face," so "eaten" is applied to "stalk" because its grain was eaten, since this meaning is known. Also among them is that the meaning of "eaten" is what is eaten, i.e., eaten by animals; it is said of anything fit for eating that it is "eaten." The meaning is: He made them like straw eaten by animals, in scattering, crumbling, and perishing. This was noted by al-Razi.
